canonical_topic: Carbon dioxide is an unavoidable product of burning organic fuel
definition: Combustion breaks the long carbon chains in organic fuels by combining carbon with oxygen, a self-sustaining exothermic reaction once ignited, which necessarily produces carbon dioxide; large-scale CO2 release can strengthen the greenhouse effect.
core_idea: Because almost all fuels are carbon-based, and combustion chemically requires combining carbon with oxygen, it is essentially impossible to burn a fuel without generating CO2.
key_points: Organic fuels are long chains of carbon molecules; combustion breaks these chains by combining carbon with oxygen.
Combustion needs an initial spark but then is self-sustaining, producing more heat than needed to start it.
CO2 is odorless and nontoxic on its own.
It is essentially impossible to burn carbon-based fuels — which is nearly all fuels — without producing CO2.
Large volumes of released CO2 can strengthen the greenhouse effect.
relationships: Two general categories of combustion pollution
caveats: Thinking CO2 itself is toxic — the author notes it is odorless and nontoxic; the risk is the climate-scale greenhouse effect, not direct toxicity.
